stops.name: Torquay surf coast
text: Torquay is where the Great Ocean Road really begins, even though the famous arch and the signage are a little further down the coast. This is surf town in the proper sense: Bells Beach is a few minutes away, the Easter surf contest there is one of the oldest in the world, and brands like Rip Curl and Quiksilver grew out of garages and sheds in this exact patch of Victoria. With around thirteen thousand residents it is a proper town, not a village, so fuel, coffee, bakeries and a good supply of wetsuit shops are all right here.

For a rider, the coast road from Torquay to Anglesea is the start of something good rather than the good bit itself. The surface is generally excellent, the corners flow with the dunes and heathland, and the sea shows up and disappears behind coastal scrub in a way that keeps your head turning. Further on, past Aireys Inlet and its lighthouse, the road begins to cling to the cliffs and the traffic begins to compete with the view. Victorian speed limits are enforced firmly and the cameras on busy holiday weekends are not shy, so treat the signed limits as real.

stops.name: Lorne
text: Lorne is where the Great Ocean Road stops being a seaside drive and starts behaving like a mountain road. The town sits on Louttit Bay with the Otway Ranges standing right behind it, steep and thick with eucalypt, tree ferns and the odd waterfall. About twelve hundred people live here, a number that swells enormously in the Australian summer holidays, when Melbourne decamps to the beach and the main street fills with surfboards and ice cream.

For a rider, Lorne is the natural place to eat. The strip along Mountjoy Parade has bakeries, cafes and fish and chips, and the pier is a good place for a coffee with a view of the bay. There is a fuel station in town, which matters because the road beyond is long, and the nearest other sizeable town back along the coast is Anglesea. Weekends and school holidays are busy, and parking a bike is easier than parking a car, though a sand-covered bay can be tricky underfoot.

stops.name: Apollo Bay overnight
text: Apollo Bay is where the Great Ocean Road takes a breath. The town sits in a curve of the Otway coast, with a long beach on one side and the wooded Otway Ranges stacked up behind, and it has about fifteen hundred permanent residents, many more in holiday season. It began as a timber and fishing settlement, and the working harbour is still there, with a fishermen's co-operative selling fresh seafood. After a day on the coast road, with its endless bends, it is a relief to stop somewhere that feels like a normal town.

The road itself has a history. The Great Ocean Road was built between 1919 and 1932 by returned soldiers from the First World War, and it was conceived as a memorial to those who died. Much of it was dug by hand and carved from steep cliffs, and the stretch east of Apollo Bay clings to the edge of the Southern Ocean with the limestone formations of the Twelve Apostles still some way to the west. Inland, the Otway rainforest is a surprise, with tall mountain ash, myrtle beech and tree ferns, fed by rainfall that is higher than almost anywhere in Victoria.

stops.name: Twelve Apostles
text: Everyone calls them the Twelve Apostles, which is generous. There were never twelve, and the original name was the Sow and Piglets, a rather less holy image that tourism officials decided to retire. Today about eight limestone stacks stand in the surf off Port Campbell National Park, and one collapsed in 2005 in front of a crowd of onlookers. The cliffs are made of soft limestone, and the Southern Ocean is working on them constantly, so the view is never the same twice.

The stacks form because waves cut caves into headlands, the caves become arches, and the arches fall to leave isolated pillars. Eventually the pillars fall too. It is a process that is visible in a lifetime, and this stretch is called the Shipwreck Coast for a reason. A short drive west, Loch Ard Gorge marks the site where the clipper Loch Ard struck the cliffs in 1878, and only two young people survived, Tom Pearce and Eva Carmichael.

stops.name: Torquay
text: Torquay is where the Great Ocean Road begins, or ends, depending on which way you ride. It is a town of about thirteen thousand people on the edge of Bass Strait, and it has a reputation that has little to do with motorcycles: this is the capital of Australian surfing. Bells Beach, a few minutes down the coast, hosts one of the world's oldest surf competitions, held every Easter, and the town gave birth to brands such as Rip Curl and Quiksilver that have since gone global. Surf World, the museum in town, tells the story with boards, photographs and a lot of sun-bleached nostalgia.

Coming back to Torquay at the end of a day on the coast is a pleasant thing. The town has everything a rider needs: fuel at several stations, supermarkets, cafes, and motels and holiday flats in all sizes. Its main street has surf shops and bakeries, and the esplanade lets you wander along the beach with a coffee and watch the surfers in their wetsuits. Jan Juc, a few kilometres away, is another surfing village that is quieter and more residential.

scout.text: Keep this if you want a coastal ride with a story behind it. About 3,000 servicemen returning from the First World War cut the Great Ocean Road's 243 km from Torquay to Allansford into a rugged coastline, and it opened in 1932 as the largest war memorial in the world. The cliffs and bends are what you see from the saddle; the history is why it is worth slowing down and stopping. Pass on it if you want an empty road or a fast run, because this is a coast to take slowly, one viewpoint at a time.

editions.lead: This Thursday: Lisbon · Sintra Ridge and Atlantic Coast. 96 km as a loop from Sintra palace roads in Portugal, about 1 h 40 min in the saddle.
editions.why: A November ride for the south: it never climbs above about 100 m, well away from the high passes that close for the winter.

stops.name: Sintra palace roads
text: Sintra is a hill town where a granite ridge catches the Atlantic cloud and holds it, so that the slopes are green, damp and cool while Lisbon, half an hour away, bakes. Lord Byron called it a glorious Eden, and Portuguese kings agreed, building summer palaces among the rocks and tree ferns. The Moors left a ruined castle on the ridge, and in the nineteenth century King Ferdinand II, a German prince who married the queen, built the Pena Palace on the highest peak, a fantasy of yellow, red and blue towers that looks as though it was assembled from a box of bricks. Close to the town centre the Quinta da Regaleira has a spiral well and tunnels, and Monserrate Palace has some of the finest gardens.

The ride up to the palaces is the point of the place. The road climbs through dense forest and moss-covered boulders in tight hairpins on a narrow, damp surface, with tourists on foot, tuk-tuks and buses sharing the road. On a busy day it can be slow and a bit nerve-racking, and the mist can fall without warning, so start early. Once you are over the ridge, the road drops west toward the sea and the cape of Cabo da Roca, the westernmost point of mainland Europe, where a lighthouse stands on cliffs above the Atlantic wind. A coast road then runs south toward Cascais, with views over surf beaches and rocky coves.

stops.name: Cabo da Roca
text: Cabo da Roca is the westernmost point of mainland Europe, a wind-scoured headland where the Sintra mountains run straight into the Atlantic and stop. The cliffs rise some 140 metres above the water, topped with a squat white lighthouse that has been working since the eighteenth century, and a stone monument carries a line from the poet Luís de Camões, who described this as the place where the land ends and the sea begins. There is something genuinely humbling about it, standing in a cold gale with nothing but ocean in front of you, though the tourist crowds have rather broken the spell by midday.

The ride in is part of the pleasure. From Sintra the road climbs through eucalyptus and cork oak into the hills, passing quiet villages and then opening onto a bare, heathy plateau. Along the coast, the N247 runs north and south with bends that are open but often sandy, and the wind can be violent, with gusts strong enough to move a loaded bike across the lane. Fog off the sea can swallow the cliffs in minutes, particularly in summer, and sometimes the whole peninsula is clear while Sintra's palaces sit in cloud. Go early, before the tour buses arrive, or late in the evening, when the sun drops into the sea.

stops.name: Guincho coast
text: Guincho is a wind machine with a beach attached. The broad, curving strand lies on the exposed Atlantic side of the Cascais peninsula, backed by dunes and a wild scrub of juniper and umbrella pine, and the north-westerly that Portuguese sailors call the nortada blows across it almost every summer afternoon. Windsurfers and kitesurfers love it, and on a good day the water is full of bright sails skimming the swell. To the north the granite bulk of the Serra de Sintra catches clouds and holds them, while to the south the line of the coast leads on toward Cascais, six kilometres away, and Alcabideche sits on the hills inland.

The dunes behind the beach are protected as part of the Sintra-Cascais Natural Park, and they are worth knowing about because they are some of the last such dunes on this stretch of coast. A boardwalk crosses the sand at Cresmina, and in spring the slopes bloom with sea lavender and wild thyme, while lizards bask on the warm planks. At the southern end of the bay, an old sea fort stands on the rocks, a reminder that this coast spent centuries watching for pirates and enemy ships.

stops.name: Cascais food
text: Cascais began as a fishing village, and the fish never left. In 1870 King Luís I made the little town his summer residence, the court followed, the aristocracy built villas along the shore, and a quiet harbour became the smart seaside resort of Lisbon. It is about thirty-six thousand people now, with a marina full of yachts, a pedestrian centre of mosaic pavements, and a fishing fleet that still unloads in the afternoon, which is the best moment to understand why people eat here.

Food is the reason for the stop, and Cascais is generous with it. Grilled sea bream, sea bass and sardines are the staples, cooked simply over charcoal with coarse salt, and you will find shellfish by the kilo, with prawns, barnacles and clams in garlic and coriander. Rice with seafood, soupy and rich, is a local classic, and a plate of salt cod in its many forms is never far away. Pastries are good, a pastel de nata for the road is almost obligatory, and the coffee is strong. Many of the best simple places are a street or two back from the water, where the prices are fairer and the customers are locals.

scout.text: Keep this if you want palaces and the edge of Europe in one short ride from Lisbon. The roads up to the Sintra palaces are narrow and steep, and access to Pena Palace is often closed to private vehicles at busy times, so park lower down rather than riding to the gate. The N247 then runs about 18 km west through the Sintra-Cascais Natural Park to Cabo da Roca, the westernmost point of mainland Europe. Pass on it at midday in high season. Keep it for an early start, before the crowds.

editions.lead: This Thursday: Blue Ridge · Asheville to Linn Cove Viaduct. 229 km as a loop from Mount Mitchell in United States, about 4 h 24 min in the saddle.
editions.why: A November ride for the south: it never climbs above about 950 m, well away from the high passes that close for the winter.

stops.name: Mount Mitchell
text: Mount Mitchell has a simple claim to fame: at 2,037 metres, or 6,684 feet, it is the highest point in the United States east of the Mississippi River. It stands in the Black Mountains of western North Carolina, part of the southern Appalachians, and a spur road climbs to the summit from the Blue Ridge Parkway at around milepost 355. The last stretch of the road ends at a car park a short walk below the summit, where an observation platform gives views across rows of blue ridges.

The mountain is named for Elisha Mitchell, a professor from the University of North Carolina who measured the peak in the 1830s and argued about its height with a rival. In 1857 he fell from a cliff near a waterfall while returning to confirm his measurements, and was buried at the summit, where his grave still lies. The area became North Carolina's first state park in 1915, after logging companies had stripped much of the forest, a loss that prompted early conservation efforts in the state.

stops.name: Linville Falls
text: Linville Falls is the most dramatic waterfall on the Blue Ridge Parkway, where the Linville River drops through a rock gorge before plunging into the wilderness below. The falls are reached by a short walk from a car park off the Parkway at about milepost 316, and several viewpoints give different angles, from the upper falls to the thundering lower cascade. Below them, the river runs into Linville Gorge, a deep canyon sometimes called the Grand Canyon of the East, which is a wilderness area with some of the wildest country in the southern Appalachians.

The Parkway itself is a masterpiece of landscape design. Built over fifty years, from the 1930s until the 1980s, it follows the crest of the mountains for almost 470 miles from Virginia to North Carolina, and was designed to give drivers a slow, scenic journey away from commercial traffic. The speed limit is low, usually 45 miles per hour, and there are no trucks, no traffic lights and no billboards, just curves, tunnels and views. The pavement is generally good, though it can be damp and covered with leaves in autumn, and you should watch for fog, which is frequent.

stops.name: Linn Cove Viaduct
text: The Linn Cove Viaduct is one of the great pieces of road engineering in the United States, and it exists because of a change of heart. The Blue Ridge Parkway, begun in the 1930s as a scenic road along the crest of the Appalachians, was nearly finished when it reached Grandfather Mountain, and the owner of the mountain refused to allow a conventional road blasted across its slopes. The solution, completed in 1983, was a curving concrete bridge that hugs the mountainside, almost four hundred metres long, built from the top down so that no heavy machinery had to cross the fragile terrain. The segments were precast and lowered into place one by one. It closed the last gap in the Parkway, which opened fully in 1987.

Riding it is a pleasure. The viaduct is an S-shape, rising and curving around the side of the mountain, with the forest falling away below, and you feel the road flowing beneath you more than you see it. Its surface is smooth concrete, with a low speed limit that is enforced and sensible, because the beauty of the place calls for slow riding. A visitor centre and a short trail let you walk beneath the bridge and see how the structure was built.

stops.name: Blowing Rock food
text: Blowing Rock is a small mountain resort on the crest of the Blue Ridge, at about 1,100 metres, and has been welcoming summer visitors since the nineteenth century, when people from the lowlands came to escape the heat. The village has a neat main street lined with shops, galleries and restaurants, with flower boxes in summer and a good deal of charm. The town takes its name from a rock formation on the edge of the gorge, where the wind blows up the cliff so strongly that, according to local legend, light objects thrown over the edge are blown back. The story that goes with it is a love story, involving a Chickasaw maiden and a chief, and is told with a straight face to children.

The Blue Ridge Parkway runs close by, and Moses H. Cone Memorial Park, with its large white manor house, carriage roads and craft centre, is only a few kilometres away. Flat Top Manor was built by a textile baron early in the twentieth century, and the carriage roads and apple orchards around it are open for walking. Nearby, the Tweetsie Railroad is a theme park built around a historic steam locomotive, a living piece of Appalachian railway history.

stops.name: Mount
text: The Blue Ridge Parkway reaches its highest point on this stretch, and the mountain at its heart is Mount Mitchell, at two thousand and thirty-seven metres, the highest summit east of the Mississippi River. A narrow spur road leaves the Parkway and climbs to a state park at the top, where a short path leads to an observation platform, and on a clear day the view runs over rank after rank of ridges, fading into blue. The summit is covered in dense spruce and fir forest of a kind more at home in Canada, a remnant of the ice age that survives on the highest peaks of the southern Appalachians, and the air smells of resin and damp.

The mountain is named after Elisha Mitchell, a professor from the University of North Carolina who measured its height in the 1830s and died in a fall near a waterfall on its flanks in 1857, which is a strange sort of fame. He is buried at the summit. The climate at the top is harsh, with cold fog, frost in most months and ice in winter, and the road is closed in bad weather.

scout.text: Keep this if you want an engineering landmark on one of America's great scenic roads. The Linn Cove Viaduct was the last piece of the Blue Ridge Parkway, finished in 1987 after the 7.7-mile section around Grandfather Mountain held the road up for two decades. It is a ride to savour rather than hurry. Stopping or walking on the viaduct is not allowed, so pass on it if you hoped to park on the bridge; keep it and take your picture from the pull-outs before it, or from the trail underneath.

editions.lead: This Thursday: Hanoi · Ha Giang Limestone Loop Stage. 416 km as a loop from Ha Giang base in Vietnam, about 8 h  in the saddle.
editions.why: December is a fine month in the tropics: ride early and late, and let the midday heat pass.

stops.name: Ha Giang base
text: Ha Giang is the last real town before Vietnam runs out of road and turns into limestone, a small, busy provincial capital on the Lo river, about as far north as you can go without crossing into China. About thirty thousand people live here, in a grid of shops, cafes, homestays and motorbike rental places that exist because of the ride that begins at the edge of town. This is where riders sleep, sort out their kit and eat a big bowl of pho before the mountains, and it is a sensible base for exactly that purpose.

The Ha Giang Loop is the draw, a few days of tight, steep, foggy mountain road through the Dong Van Karst Plateau Geopark. The road climbs from the valley through the Heaven's Gate pass at Quan Ba, past terraced rice fields and villages of the Hmong, Dao and Tay people, to Yen Minh, Dong Van and the border country at Lung Cu, where a flag tower stands at Vietnam's northernmost point. The highlight is the Ma Pi Leng Pass, a narrow shelf cut into a cliff above the Nho Que river, which runs a startling jade green at the bottom of one of the deepest canyons in Southeast Asia. The tarmac is mostly decent but narrow, with sharp hairpins, sudden potholes, mist and the odd buffalo. Take it slowly, and avoid riding at night.

stops.name: Quan Ba Heaven
text: The Heaven Gate, Cổng Trời in Vietnamese, is the pass above Quản Bạ, where the road tops a ridge at about fifteen hundred metres and the whole Dong Van Karst Plateau opens beneath it. Below, a valley of green rice terraces and small fields is dotted with the humped outlines of limestone hills, and in the middle sits the pair of round green mounds known as Núi Đôi, the Twin Mountains, which local people call the Fairy's Bosom. On a clear morning, mist lies in the hollows and the hills float above it.

This is the far north of Vietnam, a few kilometres from the Chinese border, and the country is mountain, rock and weather. The Dong Van Karst Plateau is a UNESCO Global Geopark, recognised in 2010, a high landscape of grey limestone, deep gorges and ancient fossils, and it is home to a mosaic of ethnic groups, including the Hmong, Tay, Dao and Lo Lo. Villagers farm every scrap of soil, planting maize between the rocks, and weekly markets bring colourful traditional costumes. The nearest big town is Hà Giang, about twenty-six kilometres back, where you should fill the tank and check the bike.

stops.name: Dong Van plateau
text: The Dong Van plateau is a landscape in which almost nothing is flat. In the far north of Vietnam, in Ha Giang province near the Chinese border, a vast area of limestone has been uplifted, cracked and worn into jagged grey ridges, deep valleys and pockets of terraced fields, and it is protected as a UNESCO Global Geopark. The rock is old, much of it hundreds of millions of years, and in places it is full of fossils. Maize is grown in little pockets of soil between boulders, with farmers building stone walls to hold the earth in place, so that whole hillsides look like handmade quilts.

People live here, too, in a way that seems impossible. The area is home to several ethnic minorities, including the Hmong, Lo Lo, Tay and Dao, and each has its own dress, language and customs. Villages are built of stone and clay, with thick walls against the cold, and the Sunday market in the little town of Dong Van is a riot of colour, with traditional clothing, livestock and food. In autumn, usually October and November, the buckwheat fields bloom with pink and white flowers, a gentle contrast with the grey rock.

stops.name: Ma Pi Leng Pass
text: Mã Pí Lèng is the great pass of the Ha Giang Loop, a road cut along the side of a vast gorge on the way between Đồng Văn and Mèo Vạc, and it earns its reputation in the first minute. At about fifteen hundred metres, the road clings to a cliff hundreds of metres above the Nho Quế River, which winds through a sheer, green-black canyon far below, often described as one of the deepest in Southeast Asia. The sides drop away on one hand, the mountain climbs on the other, and the colour of the river, a clear jade turquoise on a good day, is unforgettable.

The road has a story that matters. It is known as the Happiness Road, and it was built by hand between 1959 and 1965 by thousands of young volunteers and local labourers from many ethnic groups, who hung from ropes to drill and blast the cliff face with little more than hammers and dynamite, working for months at a time. A monument at the pass recognises their effort, and some of those who built it died in the work. Today it is a paved, if narrow, road, with viewing points, tea stalls and small cafés where you can sit and look across the gorge.

editions.lead: This Thursday: Clarence Drive Coastal Sweep. 264 km as a loop from Kraaifontein in South Africa, about 4 h 48 min in the saddle.
editions.why: In December the southern hemisphere is in its riding season - long days and warm roads.

stops.name: Kraaifontein
text: Kraaifontein lies on Cape Town's northern edge, where the suburbs give way to wheat fields, vineyards and the first ranges of the Boland. Its name means crow's fountain, a reminder of a time when this was a farm with a spring rather than a busy suburb on the N1. For riders, it is the threshold between the city and the Winelands.

From here, a short ride takes you into some of the most celebrated countryside in South Africa. Durbanville's wine valley is just to the west, with cellars on rolling hills. To the east, the R304 and other roads lead towards Stellenbosch and Paarl, with the great granite dome of Paarl Mountain standing over the vineyards. Beyond lies Franschhoek, founded by French Huguenot refugees in the late seventeenth century, and the Franschhoek Pass, which climbs in sweeping bends over the mountains with views back over the valley.

stops.name: Cape Town / Western Cape
text: The name Swartland means black land, from the dark renosterbos scrub that once covered the hills, and the landscape is rolling farmland, with wheat fields that turn from green to gold and then to stubble as the year goes on. In spring, particularly in August and September, the roadside verges and fallow fields explode into yellow and orange with daisies and other annuals, and the little town holds a wildflower show to celebrate it.

The coast lies about twenty kilometres west, at Yzerfontein, where the cold Atlantic washes onto long beaches and small rocky coves, so a swim is possible but bracing. Water along this coast comes from the Benguela current and is rarely above fifteen degrees Celsius, so do not expect warmth even in January. Inland, the ground rises to a ridge of granite hills, and the farm roads are mostly gravel or tarmac patched by the heat, with light traffic and long clear views.

stops.name: Atlantis
text: Atlantis is not a postcard town, and nobody here pretends it is. It was built from scratch in the 1970s on the sandy plains north of Cape Town, part of the apartheid government's plan to move coloured families out of the city and to create an industrial centre far from the suburbs. The result was a planned town of factories, schools and housing estates, some forty-five kilometres from the city, which still struggles with unemployment and crime. It is worth understanding that history as you ride through.

What the area offers is landscape. Around the town lie the Atlantis dunes, a great sea of white sand that has been used for sandboarding, quad biking and, of course, filming. The flat sandveld here is covered in tough, low scrub, part of the fynbos and strandveld vegetation of the West Coast, and in late winter and spring, roughly August and September, the plains burst into colour as wild flowers bloom after the rain.

stops.name: Constantia
text: Constantia is where wine began in South Africa, and it still has the air of a place that knows it. The valley lies on the eastern side of the Table Mountain chain, sheltered from the Atlantic, with old oak avenues, whitewashed Cape Dutch farmhouses and vineyards climbing toward the steep slopes of the Constantiaberg. It is one of Cape Town's leafiest and wealthiest suburbs, but the farms are open to visitors and the roads around it are some of the most beautiful in the city.

The story starts with Simon van der Stel, the Dutch East India Company governor, who was granted the land in 1685 and built Groot Constantia, whose gabled manor house is now a museum. A century later the farm's sweet wine, Vin de Constance, was famous across Europe: Napoleon had it shipped to him in exile on St Helena, and Jane Austen mentions Constantia wine in Sense and Sensibility as a cure for a broken heart. The style was revived in modern times and you can taste it today, along with the region's sauvignon blanc, which loves the cool breezes from False Bay.

stops.name: Near Constantia
text: The wooded eastern flank of Table Mountain rises right above this point, a few kilometres from Constantia, where the southern suburbs meet the forests and the mountain. This is Cape Town's green side: oak avenues, pine and gum plantations, old estates and the cool, shaded slopes that catch the clouds when the southeaster blows. Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden lies along the same slope, and on its terraces you can walk among proteas, ericas and other plants of the Cape Floral Kingdom with the mountain towering overhead.

The roads here wind through the trees. Rhodes Drive runs along the mountain from Constantia Nek past Kirstenbosch toward Newlands, a narrow, curving road shaded by old trees, with glimpses of the mountain through the branches. It is slow, often busy and shared with cyclists, but beautiful, especially in the early morning light. The forests of Cecilia and Newlands have walking trails up toward the mountain, and the air smells of pine, damp earth and fynbos.

stops.name: Retreat
text: Retreat sits on the flat land between the mountains of the Cape Peninsula and the sandy plains that run down to False Bay, a busy, working suburb on Main Road and the railway line south of the city. It is no beauty spot, but it lies right at the foot of some of the finest short rides in Cape Town, and its petrol stations and shops are useful when you are about to climb into the hills or head out along the coast.

The road that makes Retreat worth knowing is Ou Kaapse Weg, the M64, which starts in nearby Tokai and climbs steeply over the mountains to Noordhoek and the Atlantic side. It is a proper mountain road, with long sweepers, tight bends near the top and wide views back over the southern suburbs and False Bay. At the summit you ride through the Silvermine section of Table Mountain National Park, with fynbos on every side, and the descent to Noordhoek reveals the long white beach of Long Beach and the cliffs of Chapman's Peak. The road is popular, policed and occasionally closed for fires or accidents, so ride it with respect.

stops.name: Clarence
text: The dot sits well inland of Clarence Drive itself, on the northeastern side of Cape Town where the city thins out toward the winelands, and the ride is on its way home. Kraaifontein, a big working suburb, sits just beside it, while Stellenbosch and Paarl lie a short run to the east. The coast road that gives the ride its name, the R44 between Gordon's Bay and Rooi-Els, is hours behind you by now.

Clarence Drive deserves a few lines anyway, because it is the reason the day exists. It was carved into the foot of the Hottentots-Holland mountains, with the road clinging to the cliffs above False Bay, and it has a reputation among South African riders as the best coastal tarmac near Cape Town. The corners come in a long, rhythmic series, the sea sparkles on your left, and in winter and spring the southern right whales sometimes show up in the bay, close enough to watch from the lay-bys.

scout.text: Keep this if you want a short, intense coastal road near Cape Town. Clarence Drive runs about 22 km between Gordon's Bay and Rooi-Els, with more than 70 bends squeezed between the mountains and False Bay. It was started in 1940 and finished by Italian prisoners of war. On a clear day you can see across to Cape Point. Pass on it if you want a long day in the saddle; it is a road to ride slowly and enjoy. Keep it, use the pull-outs for photos, and watch for baboons and occasional rockfall.

264 km as a loop from Kraaifontein in South Africa, about 4 h 48 min in the saddle.

**Kraaifontein** - Kraaifontein lies on Cape Town's northern edge, where the suburbs give way to wheat fields, vineyards and the first ranges of the Boland. Its name means crow's fountain, a reminder of a time when this was a farm with a spring rather than a busy suburb on the N1.

**Cape Town / Western Cape** - The name Swartland means black land, from the dark renosterbos scrub that once covered the hills, and the landscape is rolling farmland, with wheat fields that turn from green to gold and then to stubble as the year goes on. In spring, particularly in August and September, the roadside verges and fallow fields explode into yellow and orange with daisies and other annuals, and the little town holds a wildflower show to celebrate it.

**Atlantis** - Atlantis is not a postcard town, and nobody here pretends it is. It was built from scratch in the 1970s on the sandy plains north of Cape Town, part of the apartheid government's plan to move coloured families out of the city and to create an industrial centre far from the suburbs.

**Constantia** - Constantia is where wine began in South Africa, and it still has the air of a place that knows it. The valley lies on the eastern side of the Table Mountain chain, sheltered from the Atlantic, with old oak avenues, whitewashed Cape Dutch farmhouses and vineyards climbing toward the steep slopes of the Constantiaberg.

stops.name: San José de Maipo
text: San José de Maipo is the gateway to the Cajón del Maipo, the deep river canyon that runs from the edge of Santiago into the high Andes. Only about an hour from the capital's sprawl, the town sits at roughly 970 metres, where the valley narrows and the air turns cooler and drier. Its centre is a quiet cluster of adobe and whitewashed houses with tiled roofs, a handsome church and a plaza shaded by old trees, and weekend visitors from the city fill the bakeries and restaurants. The Maipo River, brown with snowmelt, rushes below.

The valley has a long history of mining, and silver and copper were worked in the mountains above the town from the colonial period. The road that follows the canyon, Route G-25, climbs past villages such as San Alfonso and El Melocotón, where orchards and weekend cabins line the river, and onward to Baños Morales and the Monumento Natural El Morado, a protected glacier valley. Higher still, a road of gravel and sharp bends leads to the Embalse El Yeso, a turquoise reservoir built in the 1960s that supplies much of Santiago's drinking water, ringed by bare peaks.

stops.name: Embalse El Yeso
text: Embalse El Yeso is a reservoir in the high Andes, an hour or two above the last village of the Cajón del Maipo, and its colour alone is enough to make riders brake. The water is a shade of turquoise that seems artificial, held in a bowl of bare brown mountains with snow patches on the heights and the cone of Volcán San José standing guard at nearly six thousand metres. The dam was built in the 1960s to supply drinking water to Santiago, and the lake is still a vital source for the capital, which is why access is controlled and swimming is not allowed.

The approach is half the pleasure. From San José de Maipo, the road follows the river upstream through a narrowing canyon, past little settlements, orchards and hot-spring resorts, with steep walls of red and ochre rock rising on both sides. After the paved section ends, the last stretch to the reservoir is a gravel track that climbs through switchbacks to around 2,500 metres. Expect washboard, loose stones and dust, and be careful when passing vehicles. It is a route better suited to an adventure bike than a road racer.

stops.name: Baños Morales
text: Baños Morales is the last village of any size in the Cajón del Maipo, the deep, glacier-carved valley that runs east from Santiago into the high Andes, and at about 1,800 meters it feels like the end of the road. The paved road, the G-25, follows the Maipo River upstream from San José de Maipo through a canyon of red and ochre rock, with sage-green scrub, poplar groves and sudden views of snowy peaks. Beyond the village, a dirt road continues toward the El Yeso reservoir and the foot of the San José volcano, which tops 5,800 meters.

The village is small, with a handful of cabins, a modest restaurant or two and hot springs, the Termas de Baños Morales, where mineral water emerges from the mountain. A short walk leads to the El Morado Natural Monument, where a turquoise lagoon sits beneath a hanging glacier, and in summer the mountain meadows fill with wildflowers. Nearby, the old mountain hut at Lo Valdés, built in the 1930s from local stone, has long served mountaineers, and the rocks around it hold marine fossils from the Jurassic.

stops.name: Pirque
text: Pirque lies on the southern edge of Santiago, where the sprawl of the city thins out into vineyards and the Andes begin to fill the eastern sky. It is a small town with a large reputation for wine, and one of the biggest wine houses in Chile has its headquarters and original estate here. The Maipo valley, in which it sits, is Chile's classic region for Cabernet Sauvignon, and the vineyards run in neat lines toward the foothills, with the snow-capped peaks of the Andes behind them on a clear day. The setting is a lovely contrast to the busy city.

The road from Pirque leads toward the Cajón del Maipo, a deep canyon cut by the Maipo river into the mountains, and it is the natural return route for riders coming down from the Andes. Here the road passes through a landscape of orchards, vineyards and small farms, with poplars along the edges of the fields and the river valley opening toward the plain. Santiago's air can be thick with smog in winter, and a clear day after rain gives a sharp, bright view of the mountains. Evening light on the Andes, when the peaks turn pink, is one of the great sights of central Chile.

Route G-25 follows the Maipo River up through San José de Maipo; from Las Vizcachas it is about 47 km of good tarmac to the Carabineros post at San Gabriel, where you can ask about the road ahead. Beyond, about 18 km of gravel climbs to the El Yeso reservoir at around 2,500 m. Pass on the gravel if your bike does not suit it, or in winter when snow can close it. stops.name: Crown Range Road
text: The Crown Range Road is the highest sealed public road in New Zealand, topping out at about a thousand and seventy-six metres, and it connects Queenstown with Wānaka by a route that is as beautiful as it is steep. On one side, the land falls away toward the Wakatipu basin, with the jagged line of the Remarkables across the valley. On the other, the Cardrona valley opens, golden and broad, leading toward Wānaka.

The Cardrona Hotel, built in 1863 during the gold rush, still stands at the foot of the descent, with a long veranda, a garden and a reputation for good food, and it is a favourite stop for riders and skiers. The valley once held a town of thousands, and the remains of the gold workings can be seen along the roadside. In winter, the ski fields of Cardrona and Treble Cone draw crowds, and the road carries a stream of cars with skis on the roof.

stops.name: Wanaka lake
text: Wanaka sits at the southern end of its lake, with mountains stepping away to the north in long blue ranks, and the water itself is the colour of a glacier-ground gemstone. The lake is New Zealand's fourth largest and was carved by an ice tongue that once pushed down from the Southern Alps, leaving behind a deep basin and the smooth hills you ride through to get here. The town is a modest four thousand people, but it feels bigger in summer, when walkers, skiers and holidaymakers fill it, and it works neatly as a place to fill the tank, eat well and look out at the water.

The famous bit of shoreline is a lone willow growing out of the lake just by the waterfront, which has become the most photographed tree in the country. It is pretty, but it is easy to be cheeky about it, because the real beauty is everywhere else. The Clutha River, the country's largest by volume, begins right here at the lake's outlet and runs out south and east in a cold, fast, blue-green flow. Behind the town, Mount Iron and Roys Peak offer walks with views, and to the north the Matukituki valley leads towards the heart of Mount Aspiring National Park.

stops.name: Milford Road high section
text: The Milford Road does not so much climb as march into a wall. Past the beech forest of the Eglinton Valley and the long flat tussock of the Hollyford headwaters, the Darran Mountains rise in grey granite slabs on every side, and at the top of it all sits the Homer Tunnel, a rough, unlit hole in the rock that was a work-relief project for decades before it finally opened in 1953. It is just over a kilometre long and drops steeply toward the western end, and riding through it is a small adventure: cold, wet, loud, and more atmospheric than any modern tunnel has a right to be. The high section where the road approaches it is among the most dramatic stretches of tarmac in the country.

Everything here is about scale. Waterfalls hang off cliffs after rain, hundreds of metres of them, and in the right weather the whole valley is white with cascades. Kea, the cheeky alpine parrots, loiter around the tunnel entrance waiting for tourists, and they will happily unpick a seat or a bag strap if you leave your bike alone, so watch your kit. The Cleddau valley beyond the tunnel falls away in a series of hairpin bends, steep and tightening, down to the beech forest and eventually to Milford Sound itself.

stops.name: Te Anau overnight
text: Te Anau is a small town with a large job. It sits on the shore of the lake of the same name, the biggest in the South Island, and serves as the gateway to Fiordland National Park, one of the wildest places in New Zealand. About two thousand people live here year-round, many of them working in the tourism that comes through, and in summer the main street is full of campervans and people with boots and cameras.

What lies beyond is extraordinary. Fiordland is a mountainous rainforest country of glacier-carved valleys and sea inlets, shaped by some of the heaviest rainfall in the country. Milford Sound, at the end of the 119-kilometre road from Te Anau, receives so much rain that waterfalls appear by the dozen after a downpour. The Milford Road itself passes through the Eglinton Valley, with its wide flat floor and beech forest, then the Mirror Lakes, where the peaks reflect on calm water, and finally the Homer Tunnel, a rough-hewn tunnel about 1.2 kilometres long that was completed in 1953 after decades of work, with a steep descent to the sound on the other side.

stops.name: Crown Range Road
text: The Crown Range Road is the highest sealed public road in New Zealand, topping out at about a thousand and seventy-six metres, and it connects Queenstown with Wānaka by a route that is as beautiful as it is steep. On one side, the land falls away toward the Wakatipu basin, with the jagged line of the Remarkables across the valley. On the other, the Cardrona valley opens, golden and broad, leading toward Wānaka.

The Cardrona Hotel, built in 1863 during the gold rush, still stands at the foot of the descent, with a long veranda, a garden and a reputation for good food, and it is a favourite stop for riders and skiers. The valley once held a town of thousands, and the remains of the gold workings can be seen along the roadside. In winter, the ski fields of Cardrona and Treble Cone draw crowds, and the road carries a stream of cars with skis on the roof.

scout.text: Keep this if you want the highest main road in New Zealand on a clear, dry day. The Crown Range Road climbs steeply from near Lake Hayes before dropping through the Cardrona Valley, and there is only one passing bay, south of Cardrona. From May to October it is often under snow or ice and chains must be carried. Pass on it when the conditions look marginal: the Kawarau Gorge route through Cromwell is longer but safer. Keep it in the warmer months, when the climb and the valley descent can be ridden as they deserve.

editions.lead: This Thursday: SS125 Orientale Sarda. 277 km from Cagliari to Olbia in Italy, about 5 h 20 min in the saddle.
editions.why: A December ride for the south: it never climbs above about 300 m, well away from the high passes that close for the winter.

stops.name: Cagliari
text: Cagliari is a port city that grew on hills, and that is the key to understanding it. The capital of Sardinia climbs from the harbour up a steep rock crowned by Castello, the old walled quarter, which the Pisans fortified in the thirteenth century with two white limestone towers that still stand, the Torre dell'Elefante and the Torre di San Pancrazio. From the ramparts you can look across the whole gulf, the salt pans, the long white beach of Poetto and the low mountains beyond. The city's history is as layered as its streets. Phoenicians founded a port here, the Romans built an amphitheatre cut into the rock, and Aragonese and Spanish rulers added churches and palaces.

Nature is close at hand. The Molentargius salt pans, on the edge of the city, are a shallow wetland where flocks of pink flamingos feed, and they are visible from the road, which is a surprise in a city of this size. Poetto beach, about eight kilometres long, is the city's backyard, crowded in summer and almost empty in winter. Seafood dominates the menu, with bottarga, the cured fish roe, and fregola, tiny toasted pasta, appearing often. In the market of San Benedetto, one of the largest covered markets in Italy, fish, cheese and vegetables are piled high.

stops.name: Muravera
text: Muravera lies in the south-east corner of Sardinia, on the flat, fertile plain where the Flumendosa river reaches the sea. After hours of mountain road, the change of scene is striking: the land opens out into orchards, mostly citrus, with irrigation channels and small farms between the town and the coast. With about 4,400 people, it has the shops, bars and fuel you would expect, and neighbours such as Villaputzu and San Vito are only a few kilometres away. The nearest larger town is Maracalagonis, a good half hour back toward Cagliari.

The road here is the SS125, the Orientale Sarda, which runs along the eastern side of the island from Cagliari up toward Olbia. In this section it is less about the bends and more about the contrast. Behind you are the granite mountains of the Sarrabus, with their scrubby slopes of cork oak and maquis, while ahead the coast has long sandy beaches and clear water. The ride in from the mountains is a fine one, with big, flowing curves, and the surface is usually good, though patchy in places and with farm traffic and slow vans that can interrupt the rhythm.

stops.name: Baunei
text: Baunei hangs on a ledge of limestone above the Tyrrhenian sea, a town of two thousand people with the Supramonte of Baunei rising behind it and the coast far below. The SS125 comes through here on one of its most spectacular sections, climbing out of the valley from the south and then running along the face of the mountains with sea views opening on the left. The Gennargentu massif, Sardinia's highest ground, lies inland, and the whole district is one of the wildest corners of the island.

It is a place of shepherds, and a place of walkers. The Selvaggio Blu, a famous multi-day trek along the coast, starts near here and crosses terrain so steep and so remote that the walkers carry ropes. On the plateau above the town, the Golgo plateau holds a deep karst pit called Su Sterru and a small church amid the oaks, reached by a rough track, where the world feels very quiet. If you have a few hours, the road to the plateau is worth a look, though it is narrow and rough in places.

stops.name: Dorgali
text: Dorgali sits on the eastern flank of the Supramonte, the limestone massif that fills the middle of Sardinia's Nuoro province, and the town spreads over its slope with the mountains behind and the Gulf of Orosei somewhere in the haze ahead. Six thousand people live here, enough for fuel, banks and a proper choice of bars, which matters because the SS125 Orientale Sarda is a long road with long gaps. Fill the tank here and you will not think about it again until Baunei or Tortolì.

The Supramonte is a rough, dry country of white rock, holm oak and juniper, cut by deep gorges. The best known is Gola Su Gorropu, a canyon whose walls rise several hundred metres and which can be reached on foot from the road above, a walk that takes a few hours and is not for flip-flops. Not far away, the ruins of the nuragic village of Tiscali hide inside a collapsed limestone dome, a place where people lived in the Bronze and Iron Ages and, according to the story, retreated when Rome arrived. Sardinia is thick with nuraghi, those conical stone towers of the second and first millennia before Christ, and this part of the island has some of the best.

stops.name: Olbia
text: Olbia is the gateway to Sardinia for most people arriving by sea. Ferries from Genoa, Livorno and Civitavecchia dock in the long gulf, and an airport serves the Costa Smeralda, the glamorous strip of coast to the north, which the Aga Khan developed in the 1960s. The town itself is older than it looks. The Greeks called it Olbia, meaning happy, and the Romans used it as a major port; in the 1990s, when workers dug a tunnel under the harbour, they found the remains of more than twenty ancient ships. The Romanesque church of San Simplicio, in grey granite, is one of the oldest in Sardinia.

The area is Gallura, a land of granite, cork oak and low, scented scrub called macchia, with rounded boulders balanced on the hills like sculptures. Offshore, the limestone block of Tavolara island rises sheer from the sea, an eerie silhouette, and local food reflects the mix of land and sea, with seadas, fried pastries filled with cheese and drizzled with honey, and a glass of the local Vermentino white wine. Mirto, a liqueur made from myrtle berries, ends the meal.

ridingMinutes.basis: planning estimate at the ride's pace

editions.lead: This Thursday: San Francisco · Skyline, Alice’s and Pacific Return. 154 km as a loop from Skyline Boulevard ridge in United States, about 2 h 41 min in the saddle.
editions.why: A January ride for the south: it never climbs above about 150 m, well away from the high passes that close for the winter.

stops.name: Skyline Boulevard ridge
text: Skyline Boulevard runs along the spine of the Santa Cruz Mountains, high above the cities of the San Francisco Peninsula, and its ridge has a character quite unlike the coast or the bay. The road, also known as State Route 35, follows the crest through redwood and Douglas fir forest, with the fog of the Pacific on one side and the sunny, hazy bay on the other. Climbing from Belmont, about four kilometres away, you leave the suburbs behind within minutes and find yourself in cool, shaded woodland that smells of damp bark and bay laurel.

Beneath the ridge lies the San Andreas Fault, which runs through the long valley of the Crystal Springs reservoirs, the lakes that supply much of San Francisco's water. Nearby Sweeney Ridge is where in 1769 the Spanish explorer Gaspar de Portolá and his party looked down and saw San Francisco Bay for the first time, which they had missed on their march north. Redwoods in the folds of the hills include some of the oldest in the region, and many of the big trees were logged in the nineteenth century to rebuild the city.

stops.name: Alice’s Restaurant rider
text: Alice's has a second life as a rider stop, and it is worth saying a bit about the culture that has grown up around it rather than just the road. On weekends, the lot at the Skyline and Highway 84 crossing becomes a kind of open-air club, with riders from San Francisco, San Jose and the East Bay meeting for breakfast, comparing notes and drifting off in small groups. Nobody is in a hurry, and a sense of unspoken etiquette keeps things civil: park tidily, keep engines low when you leave, and wave at the locals.

The surrounding land is redwood and Douglas fir forest, in the heart of the Santa Cruz Mountains, with a thick, damp smell and a mossy hush. In the nineteenth century these hills were logged heavily to feed the growth of San Francisco, and the old skid roads and mill sites are still hidden in the trees. Many of today's roads follow those lumber routes, which explains why they bend and climb so naturally along the ridges. The San Andreas Fault runs through the valley just to the east, and the whole range is a product of the grinding collision of tectonic plates.

stops.name: Pescadero coast view
text: On the coast south of Half Moon Bay, the Pacific shows a rougher, more private face than around San Francisco, and the viewpoints here are among the best on the entire Highway 1 run. The land is a narrow marine terrace of grassland and farm fields cut by steep gullies, with sea cliffs of crumbling sandstone and long, empty beaches below. Pescadero State Beach and Bean Hollow lie a few minutes away, with tide pools full of anemones and crabs, and sea stacks standing off the shore like a row of broken teeth.

A few kilometres south is Año Nuevo, where northern elephant seals gather on the beaches to breed and moult. The breeding season runs from December to March, when the big males fight and the pups are born, and the reserve needs a booked guided walk at that time of year. Even from the highway, the huge shapes of the seals can sometimes be made out on distant sand. Gray whales pass close to shore on their migrations in winter and spring, and a patient watcher at a headland may see a spout or a flick of a tail.

stops.name: Half Moon Bay
text: Half Moon Bay is where the Peninsula's mountains finally meet the Pacific. The town sits on a wide coastal plain, backed by the green flank of the Santa Cruz Mountains and fronted by a long crescent of sand, and it feels like a different state from the busy bay side only twenty minutes away over Highway 92. Fog arrives most summer afternoons, so mornings are your best bet for sun.

Riders come through on Highway 1 and use the town as a pause on the coast run. The road here is wide and easy, with long views over fields of artichokes, Brussels sprouts and pumpkins, and it grows tighter and more dramatic south toward Pescadero and Santa Cruz. Highway 92 over the mountains is the classic way in from the east, a tight, tree-lined climb with a few steep switchbacks, and it is worth a ride in either direction. Watch for cyclists, who flock to these roads at weekends, and for the cold, wet patches under the redwoods that never quite dry out.

At Sky Londa, 1,520 ft, there is fuel and Alice's Restaurant, where riders meet. Pass on the one-lane section further south, and turn off at Highway 9 instead. Keep it for a weekend morning, with a stop at Alice's.

154 km as a loop from Skyline Boulevard ridge in United States, about 2 h 41 min in the saddle.

**Skyline Boulevard ridge** - Skyline Boulevard runs along the spine of the Santa Cruz Mountains, high above the cities of the San Francisco Peninsula, and its ridge has a character quite unlike the coast or the bay. The road, also known as State Route 35, follows the crest through redwood and Douglas fir forest, with the fog of the Pacific on one side and the sunny, hazy bay on the other.

**Alice’s Restaurant rider** - Alice's has a second life as a rider stop, and it is worth saying a bit about the culture that has grown up around it rather than just the road. On weekends, the lot at the Skyline and Highway 84 crossing becomes a kind of open-air club, with riders from San Francisco, San Jose and the East Bay meeting for breakfast, comparing notes and drifting off in small groups.

**Pescadero coast view** - On the coast south of Half Moon Bay, the Pacific shows a rougher, more private face than around San Francisco, and the viewpoints here are among the best on the entire Highway 1 run. The land is a narrow marine terrace of grassland and farm fields cut by steep gullies, with sea cliffs of crumbling sandstone and long, empty beaches below.

**Half Moon Bay** - Half Moon Bay is where the Peninsula's mountains finally meet the Pacific. The town sits on a wide coastal plain, backed by the green flank of the Santa Cruz Mountains and fronted by a long crescent of sand, and it feels like a different state from the busy bay side only twenty minutes away over Highway 92.

editions.lead: This Thursday: Tokyo · Hakone Turnpike and Fuji Lakes. 232 km as a loop from Odawara in Japan, about 4 h  in the saddle.
editions.why: A January ride for the south: it never climbs above about 1,050 m, well away from the high passes that close for the winter.

stops.name: Odawara
text: Odawara is a castle town at the foot of Hakone, and for most riders it is the place where the mountains begin. The castle, which belonged to the Hojo clan until Toyotomi Hideyoshi besieged it in 1590, has a reconstructed keep, built in 1960, with a museum inside. The old town around it is quiet, with a modest shopping street and some traditional shops. It sits on Sagami Bay, with the coast road leading east and west and the Hakone mountains rising behind.

The town is known for food. Odawara is one of Japan's great producers of kamaboko, the white fish paste cakes that appear in noodle soup and on celebration tables, and shops along the coast sell them freshly steamed. The fishing port sells dried horse mackerel, and Odawara also has a long tradition of growing ume plums, which are made into pickles and drinks. It is a pleasant place for a late lunch, with sushi bars close to the station.

stops.name: Hakone Turnpike rhythm
text: Rhythm is the right word for the Hakone Turnpike, because the road does not so much challenge you as set a tempo. Near Hakone, with Yugawara down the hill and Odawara on the coast, it climbs through broad bends that follow the shape of the old volcano, and after a few kilometres you find a steady pace in which gear changes and lean angles settle into a pattern. It is a road for enjoying rather than attacking, with smooth tarmac, clear sightlines and a limit that police take seriously.

What makes it memorable is the changing light. Cloud often rolls up from the coast and fills the valleys, so that the road climbs out of grey into sunshine, with the ridges standing like islands in a white sea. At other times the whole thing is wrapped in fog, the bends appear from nowhere, and the engine sounds louder. Take it slowly when visibility is low, and use your lights. In winter, the shaded sections can hold ice into the late morning.

stops.name: Lake Ashi view
text: Lake Ashi fills the caldera of the old Hakone volcano, at 720 metres, and it is one of the most visited places in Japan, partly because of the view. On a clear morning, particularly in winter, the cone of Mount Fuji rises above the water in perfect symmetry, and the red torii gate of Hakone Shrine stands in the lake in the foreground.

Hakone has been a travellers' stop for centuries. In the Edo period, the Tokaido, the great road between Edo and Kyoto, crossed the mountains here, and the shogun kept a checkpoint on the shore of the lake to control the passage of weapons and women. The checkpoint has been reconstructed, and a stretch of the old road, lined with huge cedars planted in the seventeenth century, still runs beside the lake. Pirate-style tourist boats cross the water, and the sulphurous steam of Owakudani, the volcanic valley above, drifts in the breeze.

stops.name: Fuji Five Lakes food window
text: Fujikawaguchiko and Fujiyoshida stand a few kilometres either side of this stop, and between them the northern face of Mount Fuji dominates everything. The Fuji Five Lakes, strung along the foot of the volcano, are the usual base for people who want a view of the mountain, and the whole district has grown up around tourism, with inns, restaurants and shops catering to hikers, photographers and bus tours. It is a busy place in season, but the food is worth the crowds.

The speciality is hoto, a thick, flat noodle stewed in a miso broth with pumpkin and vegetables, served bubbling in an iron pot. It is the signature dish of Yamanashi prefecture, said to have been eaten by the warlord Takeda Shingen's soldiers, and it is a warming meal after a cold ride. Fujiyoshida has its own noodle, a firm, chewy udon served with cabbage and a spicy paste, that is cheap and filling. Both are worth trying, and there is usually no need to book, though lunchtime queues are common.

The Hakone Turnpike, now officially the Anest Iwata Turnpike Hakone, is a privately owned toll road of about 15.8 km climbing from Odawara along a ridge above Sagami Bay. Its limit is 50 km/h, so it is a ride for the view, not for speed. At the top, the Daikanzan observation deck faces Mount Fuji on a clear day. Pass on it at weekend midday; keep it for an early start, before the haze and the car meets.

editions.title: Bainskloof and Du Toitskloof

ridingMinutes.basis: planning estimate at the ride's pace

editions.lead: This Thursday: Bainskloof and Du Toitskloof. 218 km as a loop from Constantia in South Africa, about 3 h 58 min in the saddle.
editions.why: In January the southern hemisphere is in its riding season - long days and warm roads.

stops.name: Constantia
text: The wooded eastern flank of Table Mountain rises right above this point, a few kilometres from Constantia, where the southern suburbs meet the forests and the mountain. This is Cape Town's green side: oak avenues, pine and gum plantations, old estates and the cool, shaded slopes that catch the clouds when the southeaster blows. Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden lies along the same slope, and on its terraces you can walk among proteas, ericas and other plants of the Cape Floral Kingdom with the mountain towering overhead.

The roads here wind through the trees. Rhodes Drive runs along the mountain from Constantia Nek past Kirstenbosch toward Newlands, a narrow, curving road shaded by old trees, with glimpses of the mountain through the branches. It is slow, often busy and shared with cyclists, but beautiful, especially in the early morning light. The forests of Cecilia and Newlands have walking trails up toward the mountain, and the air smells of pine, damp earth and fynbos.

stops.name: Constantia
text: Constantia is where wine began in South Africa, and it still has the air of a place that knows it. The valley lies on the eastern side of the Table Mountain chain, sheltered from the Atlantic, with old oak avenues, whitewashed Cape Dutch farmhouses and vineyards climbing toward the steep slopes of the Constantiaberg. It is one of Cape Town's leafiest and wealthiest suburbs, but the farms are open to visitors and the roads around it are some of the most beautiful in the city.

The story starts with Simon van der Stel, the Dutch East India Company governor, who was granted the land in 1685 and built Groot Constantia, whose gabled manor house is now a museum. A century later the farm's sweet wine, Vin de Constance, was famous across Europe: Napoleon had it shipped to him in exile on St Helena, and Jane Austen mentions Constantia wine in Sense and Sensibility as a cure for a broken heart. The style was revived in modern times and you can taste it today, along with the region's sauvignon blanc, which loves the cool breezes from False Bay.

stops.name: Near Cape Town
text: Few cities give you a finish line like this one. You roll into central Cape Town with Table Mountain standing over the whole bowl of the city, flat-topped and close enough to feel personal, Devil's Peak on one side and Lion's Head and Signal Hill on the other. The point on the map sits in the old centre near the Company's Garden, the patch of land the Dutch East India Company planted in the seventeenth century to supply its ships with vegetables on the way to the East.

The rides that end here, over Bainskloof and Du Toitskloof or up the West Coast to see the spring flowers, are long days, and the approach back into town is usually the N1 or N7, busy and fast. Bainskloof Pass deserves a word: it was built by Andrew Geddes Bain in the 1850s and still runs on his stone walls, a narrow, slow, beautiful road above a river gorge where you should expect gravel on the inside of bends and baboons on the parapet. Du Toitskloof is the wide modern alternative over the same mountains, with a long tunnel option for when the weather turns.

stops.name: Cape Town
text: Cape Town sits at the foot of Table Mountain, a flat-topped sandstone wall about a kilometre high, and on a day when the tablecloth of cloud spills over the edge it is one of the great sights of the world. The city lies between the mountain and the Atlantic, with a harbour that was founded in 1652 by the Dutch East India Company as a supply station for ships on the route to the East. It grew into a port of many cultures, and the mix of Dutch, Malay, African and British influences is still visible in its food, language and architecture.

Robben Island, visible from the waterfront, was where Nelson Mandela spent eighteen of his twenty-seven years in prison, and ferries run from the Victoria and Alfred Waterfront. The city centre has the Company's Garden, the Castle of Good Hope, the colourful Bo-Kaap quarter and the lively bars of Long Street. The winds can be fierce, especially the southeaster known as the Cape Doctor, which blows in summer and can make riding hard work.

stops.name: Atlantis
text: Atlantis is not a postcard town, and nobody here pretends it is. It was built from scratch in the 1970s on the sandy plains north of Cape Town, part of the apartheid government's plan to move coloured families out of the city and to create an industrial centre far from the suburbs. The result was a planned town of factories, schools and housing estates, some forty-five kilometres from the city, which still struggles with unemployment and crime. It is worth understanding that history as you ride through.

What the area offers is landscape. Around the town lie the Atlantis dunes, a great sea of white sand that has been used for sandboarding, quad biking and, of course, filming. The flat sandveld here is covered in tough, low scrub, part of the fynbos and strandveld vegetation of the West Coast, and in late winter and spring, roughly August and September, the plains burst into colour as wild flowers bloom after the rain.

stops.name: Near Stellenbosch, on the way back
Stellenbosch
text: Stellenbosch is the second-oldest European settlement in South Africa, founded in 1679 by the governor Simon van der Stel, who named it after himself and his wife's family, and it has the look of a town that has been carefully looked after. Oak trees line the streets, white Cape Dutch houses with curved gables stand behind them, and the mountains rise on every side, purple at dusk. It is also a university town, home to the Afrikaans-speaking Stellenbosch University, which gives the centre a young, lively atmosphere.

The wine country surrounds it, and the roads out are among the loveliest in the Western Cape. Head east on the R310 up the Helshoogte Pass toward Franschhoek, a village founded by French Huguenot refugees in the late seventeenth century, and the road climbs through vineyards and pine plantations, with views over the valley as it twists around bends. Other options include the Jonkershoek valley, a quiet dead-end valley full of fynbos, and the long loop over Sir Lowry's Pass to the coast. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and in the harvest season, and the Cape's winter, from June to August, is cold and wet, so spring and autumn are best.

stops.name: Bainskloof and
text: The name means wood bay in Dutch, because the early settlers cut timber from the forests in this valley to build and heat Cape Town. Today the harbour is lined with fish-and-chip stalls, and boat trips run out to Duiker Island, a rock covered in noisy Cape fur seals. Behind the village rise the sharp peaks of the Twelve Apostles and the Sentinel, a rock that looks like a sleeping giant.

The coast road from Hout Bay climbs onto the shoulder of the mountain and runs along cliffs high above the sea. Sea mist, called the Cape Doctor on the wind-blown days, rolls over the ridges, and the temperature can drop ten degrees in minutes. Around here, the mountain slopes carry fynbos with proteas and ericas, and in spring the hillsides are covered with colour. Dassies, the rock hyraxes, sun themselves on the stone walls.

scout.text: Keep this if you enjoy a narrow, historic mountain pass and can take it slowly. Bainskloof Pass was built by Andrew Geddes Bain from 1849, opened in September 1853 and is a national monument. Some sections are very narrow, with the mountain on one side and a steep drop to the river on the other, and chains at both ends keep large vehicles out. Pass on it if you want a fast, smooth road. Keep it with a relaxed pace, and expect a patchy surface in places; it was closed for repairs from 2020 to 2022.

reddit.body:
218 km as a loop from Constantia in South Africa, about 3 h 58 min in the saddle.

**Constantia** - The wooded eastern flank of Table Mountain rises right above this point, a few kilometres from Constantia, where the southern suburbs meet the forests and the mountain. This is Cape Town's green side: oak avenues, pine and gum plantations, old estates and the cool, shaded slopes that catch the clouds when the southeaster blows.

**Constantia** - Constantia is where wine began in South Africa, and it still has the air of a place that knows it. The valley lies on the eastern side of the Table Mountain chain, sheltered from the Atlantic, with old oak avenues, whitewashed Cape Dutch farmhouses and vineyards climbing toward the steep slopes of the Constantiaberg.

**Near Cape Town** - Few cities give you a finish line like this one. You roll into central Cape Town with Table Mountain standing over the whole bowl of the city, flat-topped and close enough to feel personal, Devil's Peak on one side and Lion's Head and Signal Hill on the other.

**Cape Town** - Cape Town sits at the foot of Table Mountain, a flat-topped sandstone wall about a kilometre high, and on a day when the tablecloth of cloud spills over the edge it is one of the great sights of the world. The city lies between the mountain and the Atlantic, with a harbour that was founded in 1652 by the Dutch East India Company as a supply station for ships on the route to the East.

editions.lead: This Thursday: Chile · Carretera Austral Northern Stage. 529 km as a loop from Hornopirén ferry in Chile, about 9 h 07 min in the saddle.
editions.why: In January the southern hemisphere is in its riding season - long days and warm roads.

stops.name: Hornopirén ferry
text: Hornopirén is where the road south of Puerto Montt runs out of land and hands the traveller over to the sea. It is a small port on the edge of the Reloncaví region, in front of a fjord that stretches toward Patagonia, and behind it rises the Hornopirén volcano and the dark green forests of the national park. The Carretera Austral, Chile's Route 7, passes here, and the ferry that leaves from the harbour is the only way to continue south along the highway without a long detour.

The Carretera Austral itself is a story of persistence. It was built mainly in the 1970s and 1980s by the Chilean military, who cut and blasted a road through the rain-soaked forest to connect isolated settlements, and it has been improved and extended in the decades since. The road is still a mixture of pavement and gravel, with long stretches that are rough, narrow and slow. The landscape is spectacular, with glaciers, fjords, temperate rainforest and rivers the colour of turquoise, and it draws riders from all over the world who want a proper adventure.

stops.name: Futaleufú river roads
text: The Futaleufú river is the colour of a swimming pool in a dream, an intense milky turquoise that comes from glacial silt carried down from the Andes, and it is one of the most famous whitewater rivers in the world. Rafters and kayakers come from across the globe to take on its rapids, some of which are rated at the highest level of difficulty. The river runs through a valley on the Chilean side of the border with Argentina, and the town of Futaleufú, a tidy collection of low houses with a village square, sits on its banks.

The roads here are among the least travelled in Chile, and that is what makes them special. A branch of the Carretera Austral leads to the town from the main highway, and gravel and paved sections alternate as the road follows the river through forest and farmland. Mountains rise on all sides, snow-capped in winter, and in early summer the meadows are bright with lupins. Along the way, the road passes lakes of equally improbable blue, and the light on the water in the afternoon is superb. The surfaces vary, so check conditions and keep your speed down on gravel, where loose stones and corners can surprise you.

stops.name: Hornopirén
text: Hornopirén is where the road gives up and the sea takes over. Here, on the edge of a long fjord, the Carretera Austral reaches a gap that engineers have never filled, and anyone heading south has to take a ferry for several hours through channels and inlets before the road resumes in Pumalín country. For riders coming from Puerto Montt, it is the first real taste of the end of the world: the town is small and weather-beaten, strung along the shore with wooden houses, boatyards and stacks of fishing gear.

Behind the settlement, the volcano Hornopirén rises in a neat cone, and the national park of the same name protects the forests, lakes and fjords around it. The land is wet and green, covered in temperate rainforest with ferns and mosses hanging off every trunk, and rain falls most of the year. Salmon farming dominates the economy here as it does along much of the Chilean coast, and the water is dotted with the floating pens. Mussels and other seafood are cheap and very good, and a plate of curanto, the traditional pit-cooked stew of shellfish, potatoes and meat, is the dish of the region.

scout.text: Keep this if you want a remote adventure stage rather than a polished touring road. The Carretera Austral runs more than 1,200 km from Puerto Montt into Patagonia, mixing tarmac with gravel, and parts are joined only by ferry. On this northern stage you take a short ferry before Hornopirén, and the onward ferry from there must be booked in advance. Services are thin, so carry provisions. Pass on it if you need daily fuel and food on tap. Keep it for December to March, which gives the longest days and kindest weather.

ridingMinutes.basis: planning estimate at the ride's pace

editions.lead: This Thursday: Auckland · Coromandel Peninsula Loop. 295 km as a loop from Thames in New Zealand, about 5 h 06 min in the saddle.
editions.why: In February the southern hemisphere is in its riding season - long days and warm roads.

stops.name: Thames
text: Thames is the gateway to the Coromandel, and it behaves like one, a handsome, slightly worn gold town that still has a main street of old verandahs and a stack of heritage stories. In the 1860s the strike of gold in the nearby hills brought thousands of diggers, and for a few years this was one of the largest towns in New Zealand. The mines have gone, but the School of Mines building and the mineral museum are reminders, and the long tidal flats on the Firth of Thames in front of the town are a world-class stopover for migrating shorebirds.

For a rider, Thames is the point where you decide what you need before the peninsula swallows you. The town has about seven thousand people, so fuel, groceries, repair shops and cafés are all here, and farther north the supply thins. The climb to Coromandel town runs along State Highway 25, which hugs the western shore of the Firth with the sea only a few metres from your wheels, past bays shaded by pohutukawa trees. The road is narrow and winding, with frequent blind corners, tight turns and the occasional logging truck or camper van, so ease through and use the pull-offs to let faster traffic by. In December the pohutukawa burst into red flowers, and the display is genuinely spectacular.

stops.name: Coromandel town
text: Coromandel Town is the real thing: a small, unhurried settlement of around fifteen hundred people on the west side of the peninsula, facing the Hauraki Gulf at the head of a quiet harbour. It is the last proper town before the road goes feral in the north, and it earns its place on the Auckland loop as a lunch stop and a point of arrival, since the road in from Thames is one of the great coastal rides in the country.

That road, State Highway 25, is the hero. It clings to the shore of the Firth of Thames for nearly fifty kilometres, with big pōhutukawa trees arching overhead and the tide often only a metre below the verge. In December the trees flower scarlet. It is slow, narrow and bendy enough that the average speed is low, so give it time and watch for campervans coming the other way, wide on the hairpins. After the shore the road climbs and drops over the ridge at the Coromandel Range, which has its own tight corners, then rolls down to the town.

stops.name: Whitianga beach
text: Mercury Bay is the name on the map, and Whitianga is the town that wraps around it, on the eastern side of the Coromandel Peninsula where the Pacific comes in flat and blue and rather unhurried. Captain Cook anchored here in November 1769 to watch the transit of Mercury, which is how the bay got its name, and Māori ancestors had been using the harbour long before that. The beach in front of the town is a long, gentle curve of pale sand with shallow water, the sort of beach where you can leave your jacket and boots on a bag and actually swim without negotiating surf.

You get here on State Highway 25, which on this peninsula is a road with opinions. From Thames it crawls up the Firth of Thames shore under old pōhutukawa trees, then cuts across the ranges, climbing through bush with tight, damp bends where the surface changes colour with every patch of shade. Gravel on the apexes is a regular feature after rain, and it rains with enthusiasm on the Coromandel.

stops.name: Kauaeranga valley
text: The Kauaeranga Valley runs up from the edge of Thames into the steep, wooded core of the Coromandel Peninsula, and it tells the story of the region more honestly than the postcard beaches on the other coast. Thames, about six and a half kilometres away, was a gold-rush town in 1867, and when the gold gave out the loggers turned to the great kauri forests. The valley is full of reminders. Dams built of kauri logs were used to hold water and release it in a flood to float timber down to the mill, and the remains of one, the Dancing Camp dam, can still be walked to.

Today the valley is a forest park, with the Department of Conservation visitor centre a short way up the road. The land is rugged, with volcanic ridges, rocky pinnacles and dense bush, and the road runs beside a clear stream through steep walls of green. Beyond the visitor centre the road narrows and the surface gets rougher, ending at trailheads for the Pinnacles, a famous walk to a rocky summit with a hut where trampers stay overnight. The trees are a mix of regenerating kauri, rimu and tree ferns, and the air smells of wet earth and leaf litter.

The 309 Road is a 22 km gravel road over the Coromandel Range from Coromandel town to Whitianga, narrow and twisting, with blind corners. Seven kilometres in, Waiau Falls is visible from the road, and a kilometre further a short walk leads to the most accessible stand of mature kauri on the peninsula. Pass on the 309 if your bike does not suit gravel. Keep it, ride it slowly, and stop for the falls and the kauri.
